title: When things go wrong: complaints and service recovery
vimeoName: Belong School · Module 9 · When Things Go Wrong

segments.text: Let's talk about the moments nobody puts on Instagram.
The complaint at the front desk, the dish sent back, the guest who arrives already
angry, the review that stings. If you work in hospitality long enough,
and I hope you will, these moments are guaranteed.
So instead of pretending they won't happen, let's get genuinely good at them.
First, a reframe that took me years to truly believe.
A complaint is a gift. I know how that sounds, but think it through.
A guest who complains is giving us two things, information, something in our
operation is broken, and now we know.
And a second chance, because the guest who complains to us is the guest who still
wants the stay to work. The dangerous guest is the silent one, says everything is
fine, goes home, writes the review, never returns, and we never even knew.
So when someone complains to your face, however uncomfortable, the situation is
already better than the alternative.
Breathe, and receive it like the useful thing it is. Now, the method.
When a guest is upset, there's a sequence, and the order matters.
Listen completely.
Don't defend, don't explain, don't interrupt, don't reach for the solution yet.
An upset person cannot hear solutions until they feel heard. Let them finish.
Look at them. Nod. Sometimes 30 seconds of real listening
solves half the problem, because half the problem was feeling ignored.
Acknowledge the feeling honestly.
"I'm sorry
that's not the stay we wanted you to have." You're not admitting legal fault,
you're recognizing a human being's disappointment.
It costs nothing, and it changes everything.
And please, never, ever say but. "I'm sorry, but..."
erases the apology. If there's context to explain, it can come later once things
are calm. Fix it bigger than expected.
And here's a rule I'll come back to in the final module. You have autonomy.
The cold dish doesn't just come back hot, it comes back with a glass of wine.
The room that wasn't ready earns a proper gesture, not a shrug.
The recovery should be slightly larger than the failure. Why?
Because psychology is real. A problem beautifully recovered creates more loyalty
than no problem at all. Guests forget smooth stays.
They tell everyone about the place that made a mistake and then made it
magnificently right. Follow up. The next morning, someone asks, "How
was everything last night after we sorted things out?" That 30-second question
tells the guest the care was real, not a technique.
And then this part is internal and it's non-negotiable, report it.
Every complaint goes into the system, however small, however resolved.
Not to blame anyone, because a complaint that reaches me as data is how we fix the
root cause. If three guests in a month mention the same thing, that's not three
incidents. That's one broken process wearing three costumes.
The team that hides small complaints condemns itself to repeating them forever.
A word about unfair complaints because they exist. Sometimes the guest is wrong.
Sometimes the weather is our fault in their eyes, or the expectation was
impossible.
Two things. First, you can acknowledge a feeling without agreeing with the claim.
I understand this ruined your morning is true even when we did nothing wrong.
Second, you never have to accept abuse. Rudeness, we absorb professionally.
Genuine aggression toward the team, we do not.
If a guest crosses that line, step back and call your manager.
Protecting your dignity is part of my job, and I take it seriously. And reviews.
Read them, even the harsh ones, especially the harsh ones.
A review is a complaint we didn't get to hear in person, so hear it now.
We respond to everyone, always with class, never defensively.
A future guest reading our answer to an angry review learns more about us than from
10 five-star raves. One story to close.
Years ago, a family arrived to a house that wasn't ready.
A real failure, ours, end of a brutal changeover day.
The team member at reception didn't hide behind procedure.
She sat the family on the terrace, brought drinks and pizza from the oven for the
kids, walked them through the farm to meet the animals while housekeeping finished,
and by the time they reached the house, the children were begging to stay an extra
night. That family has come back. I'm not exaggerating.
Every single year since. The mistake wasn't the story, the recovery was.
That's the standard, not perfection.
We're humans running a farm, a kitchen, and 38 houses in the Alentejo countryside.
The standard is when we drop something, we pick it up beautifully.
Next module, sustainability. Not the philosophy this time, the daily practice.
What it actually asks of you before lunch.
